title: Preparing fabric edges
subtitle: How to stop Aida and evenweave fraying before and during a project.
excerpt: Needlework fabric frays from its cut edges as it is handled and moved in a hoop. Folding the edges, taping them, or oversewing them takes five minutes at the start and prevents months of unravelling during the project.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Fabric preparation before embroidery.
Mrs Beeton, Book of Needlework (1870), Project Gutenberg #16746. Cloth preparation notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A simple hand stitch worked diagonally over the raw cut edge of a fabric to bind the threads and prevent fraying. The needle goes through the cloth from front to back, just inside the cut edge, and the thread loops over the edge each time.

content.text: Cut Aida and evenweave fray almost immediately in the hands. Preparing the edges before starting a project keeps the fabric clean and maintains the count right to the border. There are three methods: masking tape, folded hem, or
overcast edge
. Choose the one that suits your tools.
What you need
Method 1: masking tape
Cut a strip of masking tape the length of each edge.
Press it firmly along the cut edge, wrapping it to the back so it grips both faces.
Remove the tape before washing the finished piece. Masking tape leaves no adhesive residue on most needlework fabrics if removed within six months.
Method 2: overcast by hand
Thread a needle with a length of thread in a contrasting colour (easy to remove later).
Work diagonal stitches over the cut edge, passing the needle through the fabric about 3 to 4 mm from the edge each time. Do not anchor the thread; it will be removed later.
Remove the overcasting thread before mounting the finished piece.
Method 3: folded hem
Fold 1 to 1.5 cm of fabric to the back along each cut edge and press with an iron.
Tack or press the fold to hold it during the project. No needle or thread is needed if the fabric holds the fold after pressing.
Common mistakes

items.symptom: The tape leaves a sticky residue on the fabric
items.cause: The tape was left on for too long, or a high-tack tape was used.
items.fix: Use low-tack masking tape only and remove it within a few months. Remove residue with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol, then rinse in cool water.

items.symptom: The corners fray faster than the edges
items.cause: The corners were not treated when the edges were prepared.
items.fix: Apply a small square of tape diagonally across each corner, or fold the corner before folding the edges.

content.text: What this underpins
Edge preparation is the first step for any project on cut fabric.
Fabric edge preparation
also applies to the cloth margins used on scroll frames and slate frames.
